newsitem.title: THAILAND: Foreign investors wary of Thai economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors wary of Thai economic outlook.

text.p: Thailand's snap elections have given its battered stock market a major psychological boost, but most foreign investors remain wary of its short-term economic outlook.

Analysts told Reuters on Wednesday that the country's current account deficit and inflation still hovered at levels that put foreign fund managers on guard, while political uncertainty ahead of the November 17 polls represented a secondary concern.
Private economists expect Thai inflation to stay close to its 1995 level of 5.8 percent against a 5.5 percent target set by the central bank.

They said weak Thai exports would also keep the 1996 current account deficit at the 1995 level of 8.1 percent of gross domestic product, against a 7.8 percent deficit projected by the Bank of Thailand for this year.

The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) said foreign investors were net buyers of 48.6 billion baht ($1.9 billion) of Thai stocks in 1995. They accumulated another 59.5 billion baht of Thai shares in the first five months of 1996, the SET said.
Foreign sentiment, however, took a turn in June and since then foreigners became net sellers of 22.1 billion baht of Thai stocks.

"Foreign investors switched to be net sellers since June when it was clear that the economy is deteriorating. No major overseas funds have entered Thailand since mid-1995," said Thaneit Khantigaroon of Ekachart Finance and Securities.
Thaneit said no major global funds had entered South East Asian markets since mid-1995.
"What we see this week is just short-term foreign investment. No fresh major funds are coming soon. It's hoped that the economy might pick up in mid-1997," he said.

Susheel Narula, chief analyst of Seamico Securities, saw short-term foreign sentiment as weak, partly due a concern about accelerating inflation. In October, food prices are expected to post a sharp increase due to widespread flooding in Thailand.
"Foreign investment is expected to be sluggish until after a new government is formed. Foreigners are now only engaged in short-term speculation," Narula said.
